notes.meaning: David was about seventy years old, and his body was worn out from years of hard warfare, travel, and personal grief. Even when his servants piled blankets over him, he could not keep warm. His failing strength showed that his long and active reign was drawing to a close.

David's attendants suggested bringing a healthy young woman to care for him and sleep beside him. In ancient medicine, resting close to a robust, youthful person was a recognized way to restore warmth and energy to someone near death. The plan was meant to preserve the frail king's life a little longer.

The search covered all the territory of Israel until the royal servants found a beautiful young woman named Abishag. She came from the town of Shunem in the tribal land of Issachar. They brought her into the palace to become the personal caregiver for the failing king.

Abishag was extraordinarily lovely, and she faithfully cared for David's daily needs as a nurse. The text notes that David had no sexual relations with her, confirming his complete physical weakness. Even so, serving in his private room gave her an honored place in the royal household.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church father Jerome argued that taking this account literally makes little sense for an elderly king with living wives, so he explained Abishag allegorically as divine wisdom warming an aging soul.

notes.meaning: Seeing his father bedridden and helpless, David's oldest living son, Adonijah, decided to seize the throne for himself. He began acting like a monarch by gathering chariots, horsemen, and fifty royal runners to parade before him. He copied the exact royal display his older brother Absalom had once used to claim power.

David had always spoiled Adonijah and never corrected him or questioned his bad choices. On top of that, Adonijah was very handsome and was the next son born after Absalom, which made him feel entitled to rule. Undisciplined children often grow up to bring great sorrow to their parents.

Adonijah gathered support by meeting privately with Joab, the general of the army, and Abiathar, one of the leading priests. Both men were influential leaders who had grown unhappy with David and hoped to protect their own positions under a new king. With the military and part of the priesthood on his side, Adonijah gained serious political backing.

A key group of faithful leaders refused to take part in Adonijah's scheme. These loyal men included Zadok the priest, Benaiah the commander of the royal bodyguard, Nathan the prophet, and David's veteran elite soldiers. Because they had proved their steadfast loyalty to David and to God, Adonijah did not even dare invite them.

Adonijah held a massive outdoor feast near the spring of En-rogel just outside Jerusalem, slaughtering many sheep, oxen, and fattened cattle. By offering sacrifices, he tried to give his coronation a religious appearance so people would think God supported him. He invited all the other royal princes and the royal officials from Judah to celebrate his claim to the throne.

Adonijah purposely left out Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the royal bodyguard, and his younger brother Solomon. Leaving them out revealed that he knew Solomon was his true rival and that God had already chosen Solomon to reign. Eating together would have meant pledging peace, so Adonijah excluded the men he intended to push aside.

Nathan moved quickly to protect God's chosen king by going straight to Solomon's mother, Bathsheba. He asked her if she had heard that Adonijah had proclaimed himself king while David remained completely unaware. Because David was secluded in his sickroom, corrupt plots were taking place without his knowledge.

Nathan urged Bathsheba to listen closely to his plan so she could save both her life and Solomon's life. In the ancient world, a ruler who took the throne by force usually slaughtered every rival claimant and their mothers to prevent future rebellions. The situation was an urgent matter of life and death.

Nathan told Bathsheba to go directly into David's chamber and remind him of his solemn oath that Solomon would sit on the throne after him. She was instructed to ask David plainly why Adonijah was now reigning as king instead. This gentle question would prompt the king to remember his sacred duty and act before it was too late.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars suggest that David may have never actually made this earlier oath, and that Nathan and Bathsheba took advantage of the aged king's memory to secure power for Solomon.

notes.meaning: Nathan promised that while Bathsheba was still speaking with David, he would enter the chamber right behind her. His arrival would confirm everything she said with a second reliable witness. Nathan knew David's tender heart toward his sons, so a double testimony was necessary to shake the king out of his inaction.

Bathsheba entered the private bedroom where the aged king was resting under the care of Abishag. David was too weak to leave his bed or attend to royal business in public. Bathsheba respectfully set aside any personal awkwardness about Abishag's presence in order to deliver her urgent message.

Bathsheba bowed low to the ground to show great honor and reverence to David as her husband and king. David recognized her respectful posture and asked what she needed. Even in his weakened state, he was ready to hear the request of his queen.

Bathsheba reminded David that he had made a sacred promise in the name of the Lord his God. He had sworn that her son Solomon would definitely succeed him and sit on his royal throne. She appealed directly to David's personal faith and honor, knowing he would not lightly break an oath made before God.

Bathsheba then revealed the troubling truth that Adonijah had already taken over the royal title. She made sure David understood that this usurpation had happened without his permission or knowledge. Her repeated words emphasized both the shock of the treason and the king's blameless ignorance of it.

She reported that Adonijah had slaughtered many cattle and sheep for an inauguration feast and invited the royal princes, Joab, and Abiathar. Then she pointedly noted that Solomon was excluded from the gathering. Leaving Solomon out proved that Adonijah considered him a dangerous rival rather than a brother.

Bathsheba told David that all the people of Israel were waiting for his official word on who should sit on the throne next. The nation had not yet fully sided with Adonijah because they recognized David's authority as God's prophet-king to name his successor. A single clear declaration from David would settle the entire crisis immediately.

She warned David of the terrible fate awaiting her family once he passed away. If Adonijah kept the crown, he would brand Solomon and Bathsheba as traitors and execute them to secure his rule. She pleaded with him as a mother fighting for the survival of herself and her son.

Right on schedule, while Bathsheba was still finishing her appeal, Nathan the prophet arrived at the royal chamber. His timely appearance fulfilled his promise to support her plea and bring the matter to a swift decision. As a matter of royal court manners, Bathsheba stepped aside so the king could grant a private audience to the prophet.

The palace attendants announced Nathan, and he walked in and bowed facedown to the floor before the bedridden king. Nathan showed David the same deep honor and royal respect in his sickbed as he would have on a golden throne. True godly leaders always honor the authority God has established over them.

Nathan boldly asked the king if he had secretly authorized Adonijah to become the next ruler. His direct question challenged David to clear his own name from any part in the rebellion. Nathan knew God had promised the kingdom to Solomon, so he spoke frankly to stir the tired king into action.

Nathan described the festive gathering where animals were slaughtered in abundance and the army commanders and priests were dining with Adonijah. The crowd was already drinking and shouting, 'Long live King Adonijah,' treating David as if he were already gone. This vivid report showed David how far the treason had progressed in just one day.

Nathan closed his testimony by pointing out that Adonijah had excluded Nathan, Zadok the priest, Benaiah, and Solomon from the celebration. This deliberate snub proved that Adonijah had no intention of consulting God's prophet or honoring David's closest servants. It showed beyond doubt that the uprising was an open defiance of both God's plan and the king's house.
